claim: RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) transcription initiates bidirectionally at many human protein-coding genes.
source: RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) transcription initiates bidirectionally at many human protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sense transcription usually dominates and leads to messenger RNA production at bidirectional promoters.
source: Sense transcription usually dominates and leads to messenger RNA production, whereas antisense transcription rapidly terminates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bidirectional transcription supported by the manuscript's experimental findings.

claim: Antisense transcription rapidly terminates at bidirectional promoters.
source: Sense transcription usually dominates and leads to messenger RNA production, whereas antisense transcription rapidly terminates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by POINT-seq data showing limited antisense transcription extension.

claim: Sense transcriptional initiation is more efficient than in the antisense direction.
source: Here, we show that sense transcriptional initiation is more efficient than in the antisense direction, which establishes initial promoter directionality.
evidence: This is supported by sPOINT-seq data showing higher signal in the sense direction (Figure 3).

claim: INTS11 terminates antisense transcription.
source: Specifically, INTS11 terminates antisense transcription, whereas sense transcription is protected from INTS11-dependent attenuation by CDK9 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by POINT-seq showing increased antisense transcription upon INTS11 depletion (Figure 2).

claim: Sense transcription is protected from INTS11-dependent attenuation by CDK9 activity.
source: Specifically, INTS11 terminates antisense transcription, whereas sense transcription is protected from INTS11-dependent attenuation by CDK9 activity.
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq demonstrating that CDK9 inhibition sensitizes sense transcription to INTS11 (Figure 4).

claim: INTS11 attenuates transcription in both directions upon CDK9 inhibition.
source: Strikingly, INTS11 attenuates transcription in both directions upon CDK9 inhibition, and the engineered recruitment of CDK9 desensitises transcription to INTS11.
evidence: This is demonstrated by POINT-seq showing bidirectional transcription increase when both CDK9 is inhibited and INTS11 is depleted (Figure 4).

claim: Engineered recruitment of CDK9 desensitizes transcription to INTS11.
source: Strikingly, INTS11 attenuates transcription in both directions upon CDK9 inhibition, and the engineered recruitment of CDK9 desensitises transcription to INTS11.
evidence: This is shown by HIV reporter experiments where TAT-mediated CDK9 recruitment reduces INTS11 sensitivity (Figure 4F).

claim: Similar asymmetry in bidirectional transcription frequently occurs in unicellular eukaryotes (e.g. budding yeast).
source: Similar asymmetry frequently occurs in unicellular eukaryotes (e.g. budding yeast) and at some plant promoters (Wyers et al., 2005; Thieffry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Similar asymmetry in bidirectional transcription occurs at some plant promoters.
source: Similar asymmetry frequently occurs in unicellular eukaryotes (e.g. budding yeast) and at some plant promoters (Wyers et al., 2005; Thieffry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bidirectionality is the ground state of promoters.
source: Interestingly, bidirectionality is the ground state of promoters and directionality is acquired over evolutionary time (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Directionality is acquired over evolutionary time.
source: Interestingly, bidirectionality is the ground state of promoters and directionality is acquired over evolutionary time (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Directionality is acquired through a combination of DNA sequences and proteins that favour the directional initiation and elongation of transcription.
source: This is proposed to be through a combination of DNA sequences and proteins that favour the directional initiation and elongation of transcription.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on evolutionary studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: U1 snRNA promotes RNAPII elongation through protein-coding genes by binding to RNA and preventing early termination.
source: U1 snRNA promotes RNAPII elongation through protein-coding genes by binding to RNA and preventing early termination (Kaida et al., 2010; Mimoso and Adelman, 2023; Chiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: RNA-bound U1 prevents early termination by inhibiting PASs and antagonising other attenuation mechanisms.
source: RNA-bound U1 prevents early termination by inhibiting PASs and antagonising other attenuation mechanisms, which include those involving the PP1-PNUTS phosphatase and Restrictor complexes (So et al., 2019; Estell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: U1 binding sites are rarer within short antisense transcripts.
source: In contrast, U1 binding sites are rarer within short antisense transcripts, which are often rich in PAS sequences that are proposed to promote transcriptional termination (Almada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Short antisense transcripts are often rich in PAS sequences that are proposed to promote transcriptional termination.
source: In contrast, U1 binding sites are rarer within short antisense transcripts, which are often rich in PAS sequences that are proposed to promote transcriptional termination (Almada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The Integrator complex comprises the backbone, arm/tail, phosphatase, and endonuclease modules.
source: The Integrator complex comprises the backbone, arm/tail, phosphatase, and endonuclease modules (Wagner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: INTS11 is the endoribonuclease of the Integrator complex.
source: Its endoribonuclease is INTS11, and its phosphatase activity is mediated by an association between INTS6 and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Integrator complex composition.

claim: Integrator phosphatase activity is mediated by an association between INTS6 and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A).
source: Its endoribonuclease is INTS11, and its phosphatase activity is mediated by an association between INTS6 and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Integrator complex function.

claim: Loss of the INTS11 endonuclease broadly affects promoter-proximal transcriptional attenuation.
source: Loss of the INTS11 endonuclease broadly affects promoter-proximal transcriptional attenuation, whereas INTS6-PP2A activity is proposed to regulate the escape of RNAPII into elongation (Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: INTS6-PP2A activity is proposed to regulate the escape of RNAPII into elongation.
source: Loss of the INTS11 endonuclease broadly affects promoter-proximal transcriptional attenuation, whereas INTS6-PP2A activity is proposed to regulate the escape of RNAPII into elongation (Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: INTS6-PP2A phosphatase functionally antagonises CDK9.
source: INTS6-PP2A phosphatase functionally antagonises CDK9, which is vital for RNAPII promoter escape and productive elongation (Vervoort et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: CDK9 is vital for RNAPII promoter escape and productive elongation.
source: INTS6-PP2A phosphatase functionally antagonises CDK9, which is vital for RNAPII promoter escape and productive elongation (Vervoort et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and is established knowledge.

claim: RBBP6 is required to activate the PAS cleavage machinery.
source: Because RBBP6 is required to activate the PAS cleavage machinery (Schmidt et al., 2022; Boreikaite et al., 2022), its depletion should inhibit any PAS-dependent transcriptional termination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RBBP6 depletion should inhibit any PAS-dependent transcriptional termination.
source: Because RBBP6 is required to activate the PAS cleavage machinery (Schmidt et al., 2022; Boreikaite et al., 2022), its depletion should inhibit any PAS-dependent transcriptional termination.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on RBBP6's known function.

claim: Tagged RBBP6 was efficiently depleted after exposure to the dTAGv-1 degrader.
source: Three homozygous dTAG-RBBP6 clones were isolated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and tagged RBBP6 was efficiently depleted after exposure to the dTAGv-1 degrader (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot in Figure 1A.

claim: RBBP6 depletion induces a transcriptional termination defect in the protein-coding direction downstream of the PAS at NEDD1.
source: RBBP6 depletion induces a transcriptional termination defect in the protein-coding direction (downstream of the indicated PAS) but not the upstream antisense direction.
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq genome browser track at NEDD1 in Figure 1B.

claim: RBBP6 depletion does not affect upstream antisense transcription at NEDD1.
source: RBBP6 depletion induces a transcriptional termination defect in the protein-coding direction (downstream of the indicated PAS) but not the upstream antisense direction.
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq genome browser track at NEDD1 in Figure 1B.

claim: RBBP6 loss causes a general increase in transcription downstream of the sense gene PAS.
source: Meta-analysis of this data on genes separated from their neighbours by ≥10 kb shows that RBBP6 loss causes a general increase in transcription downstream of the sense gene PAS but has little effect on upstream antisense transcription (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metaplot and heatmap analysis in Figure 1C and D.

claim: RBBP6 loss has little effect on upstream antisense transcription.
source: Meta-analysis of this data on genes separated from their neighbours by ≥10 kb shows that RBBP6 loss causes a general increase in transcription downstream of the sense gene PAS but has little effect on upstream antisense transcription (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by metaplot and heatmap analysis in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Many antisense transcripts contain multiple AAUAAA PAS sequences.
source: Although many antisense transcripts contain multiple AAUAAA PAS sequences that could aid termination, our POINT-seq experiment suggests that RBBP6 depletion has limited impact on the transcription of these RNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown by analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: RBBP6 depletion has limited impact on the transcription of antisense RNAs containing AAUAAA PAS sequences.
source: Although many antisense transcripts contain multiple AAUAAA PAS sequences that could aid termination, our POINT-seq experiment suggests that RBBP6 depletion has limited impact on the transcription of these RNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by POINT-seq heatmap analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: XRN2 does not affect antisense transcriptional termination.
source: Similarly, we recently showed that the PAS-dependent 5′→3′ exonucleolytic torpedo terminator, XRN2, does not affect antisense transcriptional termination (Estell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Most antisense transcription appears to terminate using PAS-independent mechanisms.
source: Therefore, although some antisense transcripts are polyadenylated, most antisense transcription appears to terminate using PAS-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the RBBP6 depletion experiments showing limited effect on antisense transcription.

claim: PAS-dependent termination cannot fully explain the promoter-proximal attenuation of antisense transcription.
source: Consequently, PAS-dependent termination cannot fully explain the promoter-proximal attenuation of antisense transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the RBBP6 depletion experiments.

claim: Integrator was first identified as the 3′ end processing complex for snRNAs.
source: A major PAS-independent termination pathway is controlled by the Integrator complex, which was first identified as the 3′ end processing complex for snRNAs (Baillat et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Integrator terminates transcription from most other RNAPII promoters, including those that initiate antisense transcription.
source: Several more recent reports show that Integrator also terminates transcription from most other RNAPII promoters, including those that initiate antisense transcription, so it might affect promoter directionality (Wagner et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: INTS11 depletion causes a clear extension of POINT-seq read density at RNU5A-1 and RNU5B-1 loci.
source: Integrator is established to control the transcription of snRNAs (Baillat et al., 2005), and this was detected in our POINT-seq, which demonstrates a clear extension of POINT-seq read density at RNU5A-1 and RNU5B-1 loci (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by genome browser tracks in Figure 2B.

claim: INTS11 loss does not affect the termination of protein-coding transcription at PGK1.
source: As exemplified by PGK1 (Figure 2C), INTS11 loss does not affect the termination of protein-coding transcription but causes a strong upregulation of upstream antisense transcription.
evidence: This is shown by genome browser track in Figure 2C.

claim: INTS11 loss causes a strong upregulation of upstream antisense transcription at PGK1.
source: As exemplified by PGK1 (Figure 2C), INTS11 loss does not affect the termination of protein-coding transcription but causes a strong upregulation of upstream antisense transcription.
evidence: This is shown by genome browser track in Figure 2C.

claim: INTS11 frequently attenuates antisense transcription.
source: Overall, INTS11 frequently attenuates antisense transcription, whereas a smaller fraction of sense transcription is affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by metaplot and heatmap analyses in Figure 2D and E.

claim: A smaller fraction of sense transcription is affected by INTS11 compared to antisense transcription.
source: Overall, INTS11 frequently attenuates antisense transcription, whereas a smaller fraction of sense transcription is affected.
evidence: This is demonstrated by metaplot and heatmap analyses in Figure 2.

claim: The most strongly affected protein-coding genes by INTS11 are lowly expressed genes.
source: The most strongly affected examples of this are lowly expressed genes, which is consistent with recent findings (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Lykke-Andersen et al., 2021; Beckedorff et al., 2020; Tatomer et al., 2019; Elrod et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown by scatter plot analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations.

claim: When both directions at head-to-head promoters are protein-coding, INTS11 depletion causes modest reductions in the metaplot POINT-seq signal.
source: In the former case, transcription will be bi-directionally elongated with both transcripts resembling those synthesised in the sense direction at directional promoters. In the latter case, transcription in both directions is rapidly attenuated as is the case for upstream antisense transcription at directional promoters. When both directions are protein-coding, INTS11 depletion causes modest reductions in the metaplot POINT-seq signal as was the case for sense transcription in Figure 2D (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by metaplot analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: eRNA transcription is upregulated upon INTS11 elimination.
source: Conversely, eRNA transcription is upregulated upon INTS11 elimination as was the case for antisense transcription in Figure 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by metaplot analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Short ncRNAs are more strongly affected by INTS11 than protein-coding transcripts.
source: We conclude that short ncRNAs are more strongly affected by INTS11 than protein-coding transcripts.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing effects on different transcript types in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: sPOINT effectively captures and assays the promoter-proximal RNAPII pause.
source: Since most capped RNAPII-associated RNA < 150 nts maps to promoter-proximal regions, we suggest that sPOINT effectively captures and assays the well-characterised promoter-proximal RNAPII pause.
evidence: This is inferred from the restricted TSS-proximal signal shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: sPOINT-seq shows a higher signal in the sense direction in unperturbed cells.
source: The sPOINT-seq metaplot in Figure 3C shows a higher signal in the sense direction in unperturbed cells, suggesting that more efficient transcriptional initiation helps to explain promoter directionality.
evidence: This is shown by metaplot analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: More efficient transcriptional initiation helps to explain promoter directionality.
source: The sPOINT-seq metaplot in Figure 3C shows a higher signal in the sense direction in unperturbed cells, suggesting that more efficient transcriptional initiation helps to explain promoter directionality.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher sense signal in sPOINT-seq data.

claim: Sense transcription initiates in a more focused manner compared to the antisense direction.
source: In addition, the lower TSS mapped plot indicates that sense transcription initiates in a more focused manner compared to in the antisense direction.
evidence: This is shown by the sharp sense TSS peak versus dispersed antisense TSSs in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Antisense TSSs are more dispersed than sense TSSs.
source: This is because a sharp sense TSS peak is evident in the lower plot of Figure 3D, whereas antisense TSSs are more dispersed.
evidence: This is shown by sPOINT-seq TSS mapping in Figure 3D-F.

claim: INTS11 loss caused a mild reduction in sPOINT-seq signal.
source: INTS11 loss caused a mild reduction in sPOINT-seq signal, suggesting that the enhanced antisense transcription seen after its elimination is not because transcriptional initiation is increased.
evidence: This is shown by sPOINT-seq metaplot in Figure 3D.

claim: The enhanced antisense transcription seen after INTS11 elimination is not because transcriptional initiation is increased.
source: INTS11 loss caused a mild reduction in sPOINT-seq signal, suggesting that the enhanced antisense transcription seen after its elimination is not because transcriptional initiation is increased.
evidence: This is inferred from the sPOINT-seq data showing reduced signal upon INTS11 loss.

claim: The slight reduction in sPOINT-seq signal upon INTS11 loss could result from less transcriptional initiation or because INTS11 loss allows more RNAPII to escape the promoter.
source: This slight reduction in sPOINT-seq signal could result from less transcriptional initiation or be because INTS11 loss allows more RNAPII to escape the promoter and elongate transcripts beyond the ~150 nt length detectable by sPOINT-seq.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying the observed signal reduction.

claim: INTS11 affects transcription very early.
source: INTS11 affects transcription very early, occupies promoters, and becomes less active as RNAPII moves into elongation (Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022; Vervoort et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2020; Ramamurthy et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: INTS11 occupies promoters.
source: INTS11 affects transcription very early, occupies promoters, and becomes less active as RNAPII moves into elongation (Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022; Vervoort et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2020; Ramamurthy et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: INTS11 becomes less active as RNAPII moves into elongation.
source: INTS11 affects transcription very early, occupies promoters, and becomes less active as RNAPII moves into elongation (Hu et al., 2023; Stein et al., 2022; Vervoort et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2020; Ramamurthy et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The phosphorylation of RNAPII and other factors by CDK9 releases promoter-proximally paused RNAPII into elongation.
source: One of the first transcriptional checkpoints involves the phosphorylation of RNAPII and other factors by CDK9, which releases promoter-proximally paused RNAPII into elongation (Fujinaga et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and is established knowledge.

claim: The Integrator-associated phosphatase, PP2A, antagonises CDK9.
source: During this process, the Integrator-associated phosphatase, PP2A, antagonises CDK9 and presumably regulates the sensitivity of RNAPII to INTS11 (Vervoort et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Integrator phosphatase has little effect on antisense transcription.
source: Because Integrator phosphatase has little effect on antisense transcription (Hu et al., 2023), we hypothesised that INTS11 sensitivity and CDK9 activity are inversely correlated to maintain directionality after initiation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: INTS11 sensitivity and CDK9 activity are inversely correlated to maintain directionality after initiation.
source: Because Integrator phosphatase has little effect on antisense transcription (Hu et al., 2023), we hypothesised that INTS11 sensitivity and CDK9 activity are inversely correlated to maintain directionality after initiation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental observations.

claim: Sense transcription will be attenuated via INTS11 when CDK9 is inactive.
source: Our hypothesis predicts that sense transcription will be attenuated via INTS11 when CDK9 is inactive.
evidence: This is a prediction from the authors' hypothesis, tested experimentally.

claim: CDK9i treatment reduced transcription over the protein-coding gene body at TARDBP.
source: As expected, CDK9i treatment reduced transcription over the protein-coding gene body.
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq genome browser track in Figure 4A.

claim: Antisense transcription displays CDK9 sensitivity.
source: Antisense transcription also displays CDK9 sensitivity.
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq data in Figure 4.

claim: In CDK9i-treated cells, INTS11 loss increased transcription in both directions.
source: Importantly, in CDK9i-treated cells, INTS11 loss increased transcription in both directions.
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq data in Figure 4A-D.

claim: CDK9 activity prevents sense transcription from being attenuated by INTS11.
source: As such, CDK9 activity prevents sense transcription from being attenuated by INTS11.
evidence: This is concluded from the POINT-seq experiments showing bidirectional sensitivity to INTS11 when CDK9 is inhibited.

claim: When CDK9 and INTS11 are both compromised, the POINT-seq signal remains higher in the sense vs. antisense direction.
source: Importantly, when CDK9 and INTS11 are both compromised, the POINT-seq signal remains higher in the sense vs. antisense direction (black line, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by metaplot analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Sense transcription initiates more efficiently than antisense transcription.
source: This is consistent with our sPOINT-based finding that sense transcription initiates more efficiently than antisense transcription.
evidence: This is supported by sPOINT-seq data in Figure 3.

claim: Following CDK9 inhibition and INTS11 loss, the largest recovery of protein-coding transcription is often over the 5′ end of genes.
source: While the effects of INTS11 and CDK9 activities are the clearest on antisense and sense transcription, respectively, this is not binary. Some antisense transcription is lost upon CDK9 inhibition, which indicates CDK9 activity on some antisense RNAPII (Figure 4 and Fong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is observed in POINT-seq data in Figure 4.

claim: Some antisense transcription is lost upon CDK9 inhibition.
source: Some antisense transcription is lost upon CDK9 inhibition, which indicates CDK9 activity on some antisense RNAPII (Figure 4 and Fong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is shown by POINT-seq data in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: CDK9 activity occurs on some antisense RNAPII.
source: Some antisense transcription is lost upon CDK9 inhibition, which indicates CDK9 activity on some antisense RNAPII (Figure 4 and Fong et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some antisense transcription is CDK9-sensitive.

claim: CDK9i treatment suppresses Ser2p on RNAPII.
source: As previously shown (Olson et al., 2018), CDK9i treatment suppresses Ser2p.
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 4E and supported by citation.

claim: Both Ser5p and Ser2p are enhanced by INTS11 loss whether CDK9 is active or not.
source: However, both Ser5p and Ser2p are enhanced by INTS11 loss whether CDK9 is active or not.
evidence: This is shown by western blot in Figure 4E.

claim: Unattenuated transcription resulting from INTS11 depletion is associated with some CTD phosphorylation.
source: Thus, unattenuated transcription resulting from INTS11 depletion is associated with some CTD phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blot data showing maintained phosphorylation upon INTS11 loss.

claim: Where CDK9i is employed, kinases that are functionally redundant with CDK9 presumably phosphorylate RNAPII.
source: Where CDK9i is employed, kinases that are functionally redundant with CDK9 presumably phosphorylate RNAPII.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain maintained phosphorylation when CDK9 is inhibited.

claim: Inhibition of CDK7 with THZ2 sensitised selected protein-coding transcripts to INTS11 attenuation.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of CDK7 with THZ2 also sensitised the same selected protein-coding transcripts to INTS11 attenuation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CDK7 is required to activate CDK9.
source: This may be because CDK7 is required to activate CDK9 (Larochelle et al., 2012) or because Integrator additionally targets RNAPII when CDK7 is inactive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Integrator may additionally target RNAPII when CDK7 is inactive.
source: This may be because CDK7 is required to activate CDK9 (Larochelle et al., 2012) or because Integrator additionally targets RNAPII when CDK7 is inactive.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of CDK7 inhibition effects.

claim: Transcription from the HIV promoter results in synthesis of the trans-activating response (TAR) element and promoter proximal RNAPII pausing.
source: Transcription from the HIV promoter results in synthesis of the trans-activating response (TAR) element and promoter proximal RNAPII pausing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV transcription.

claim: Pause release from the HIV promoter requires TAT, which promotes RNAPII elongation by recruiting CDK9 via TAR.
source: Pause release requires the trans-activator of transcription (TAT), which promotes RNAPII elongation by recruiting CDK9 via TAR (Wei et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work and is established knowledge.

claim: INTS11 suppresses transcription from the HIV promoter when TAT is absent.
source: INTS11 suppresses transcription from the HIV promoter when TAT is absent (Stadelmayer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: INTS11 loss induces HIV transcription in the absence of TAT.
source: As expected, INTS11 loss induces HIV transcription in the absence of TAT.
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: TAT strongly stimulates HIV transcription (~200-fold).
source: However, TAT strongly stimulates transcription (~200-fold) and desensitises it to INTS11 loss.
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: TAT desensitises HIV transcription to INTS11 loss.
source: However, TAT strongly stimulates transcription (~200-fold) and desensitises it to INTS11 loss.
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: TAT-mediated CDK9 recruitment alleviates INTS11-dependent attenuation of transcription.
source: Therefore, TAT-mediated CDK9 recruitment alleviates INTS11-dependent attenuation of transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the HIV reporter experiments showing reduced INTS11 sensitivity with TAT.

claim: CDK9 inhibition sensitises TAT-activated transcription to INTS11.
source: Similar to endogenous protein-coding genes, CDK9 inhibition sensitises TAT-activated transcription to INTS11 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CDK9 activity counteracts transcriptional attenuation by INTS11.
source: Overall, our data strongly suggest that CDK9 activity counteracts transcriptional attenuation by INTS11.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experiments including POINT-seq and HIV reporter assays.

claim: Preferential sense transcriptional initiation significantly contributes towards the directionality of many mammalian promoters.
source: However, we show that preferential sense transcriptional initiation significantly contributes towards the directionality of many mammalian promoters.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sPOINT-seq data showing higher sense initiation.

claim: A unidirectional arrangement of at least some core promoter elements favours transcription in the protein-coding direction.
source: More analyses are required to elucidate the mechanism, but we hypothesise that a unidirectional arrangement of at least some core promoter elements favours transcription in the protein-coding direction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The evolution of promoter elements helps explain how a bidirectional promoter 'ground state' acquired directionality in yeast.
source: Consistently, the evolution of promoter elements helps explain how a bidirectional promoter 'ground state' acquired directionality in yeast (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: More focused transcription initiation is associated with highly expressed mammalian genes.
source: More focused transcription initiation is also associated with highly expressed mammalian genes and with promoters that have clearly defined elements (e.g. TATA) (Rengachari et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: More focused transcription initiation is associated with promoters that have clearly defined elements (e.g. TATA).
source: More focused transcription initiation is also associated with highly expressed mammalian genes and with promoters that have clearly defined elements (e.g. TATA) (Rengachari et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The lower level and dispersed nature of antisense initiation may reflect the suboptimal orientation of promoter elements or the opportunistic transcription of open chromatin in promoter regions.
source: Thus, the lower level and dispersed nature of antisense initiation may reflect the suboptimal orientation of promoter elements or the opportunistic transcription of open chromatin in promoter regions.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of dispersed antisense initiation.

claim: INTS11 controls transcriptional attenuation via its endonuclease activity.
source: We hypothesise that INTS11 controls transcriptional attenuation via its endonuclease activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: An inactive mutant of INTS11 (E203Q) poorly associates with other Integrator components compared to wild-type INTS11.
source: An inactive mutant of INTS11 (E203Q) is widely used to interrogate its catalytic function (Baillat et al., 2005); however, we found that it poorly associates with other Integrator components compared to wild-type INTS11 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Catalytic mutations in CPSF73 disrupt its association with other cleavage and polyadenylation components.
source: Similarly, catalytic mutations in the highly related PAS endonuclease, CPSF73, disrupt its association with other cleavage and polyadenylation components (Kolev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: INTS11 and SPT5 are adjacent in the RNAPII: Integrator structure.
source: How CDK9 activity opposes INTS11 is unresolved, but INTS11 and SPT5 are adjacent in the RNAPII: Integrator structure (Fianu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published structural work.

claim: SPT5 is a prominent substrate of CDK9.
source: As SPT5 is a prominent substrate of CDK9 (Yamada et al., 2006; Cortazar et al., 2019; Parua et al., 2018), its phosphorylation might evict INTS11 or prevent its association with the complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SPT5 phosphorylation might evict INTS11 or prevent its association with the RNAPII complex.
source: As SPT5 is a prominent substrate of CDK9 (Yamada et al., 2006; Cortazar et al., 2019; Parua et al., 2018), its phosphorylation might evict INTS11 or prevent its association with the complex.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of CDK9-mediated protection from INTS11.

claim: Integrator is enriched on promoters.
source: Consistently, Integrator is enriched on promoters, whereas phosphorylated SPT5 (SPT5p) is most prevalent during elongation over protein-coding gene bodies (Zheng et al., 2020; Cortazar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylated SPT5 (SPT5p) is most prevalent during elongation over protein-coding gene bodies.
source: Consistently, Integrator is enriched on promoters, whereas phosphorylated SPT5 (SPT5p) is most prevalent during elongation over protein-coding gene bodies (Zheng et al., 2020; Cortazar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Antisense transcription increased by INTS11 loss is not accompanied by increased Ser5p and Ser2p.
source: Furthermore, although antisense transcription is increased by INTS11 loss, published data suggest that this is not accompanied by increased Ser5p and Ser2p (Hu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Ser5p and Ser2p RNAPII modifications require CDK7 and CDK9.
source: As these RNAPII modifications require CDK7 and CDK9, this provides further support that these activities are less prevalent for antisense vs. sense transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinases responsible for CTD phosphorylation.

claim: CDK7 and CDK9 activities are less prevalent for antisense vs. sense transcription.
source: As these RNAPII modifications require CDK7 and CDK9, this provides further support that these activities are less prevalent for antisense vs. sense transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that antisense transcription lacks these phosphorylation marks.

claim: Some antisense transcription undergoes INTS11-independent attenuation.
source: Such CDK9-sensitive antisense transcription could undergo INTS11-independent attenuation, which might account for the polyadenylated antisense RNA observed previously (Almada et al., 2013; Flynn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning to explain CDK9-sensitive antisense transcription.

claim: Some antisense transcription is targeted by the poly(A) exosome targeting connection.
source: Consistently, some antisense transcription is targeted by the poly(A) exosome targeting connection, which operates on polyadenylated transcripts (Wu et al., 2020; Meola et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Restrictor complex restrains antisense transcription.
source: We and others recently described the Restrictor complex as restraining antisense transcription (Estell et al., 2023; Estell et al., 2021; Austenaa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' and others' published work.

claim: Integrator associates with NELF-bound RNAPII.
source: Unlike Integrator, which associates with NELF-bound RNAPII (Fianu et al., 2021), Restrictor is proximal to the distinct PAF-bound RNAPII (Estell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published structural work.

claim: Restrictor is proximal to PAF-bound RNAPII.
source: Unlike Integrator, which associates with NELF-bound RNAPII (Fianu et al., 2021), Restrictor is proximal to the distinct PAF-bound RNAPII (Estell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' published work.

claim: Various complexes may target different forms of RNAPII before and after CDK9 activity.
source: Thus, various complexes may target different forms of RNAPII before and after CDK9 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the different associations of Integrator and Restrictor with RNAPII.

claim: Integrator influences a greater volume of antisense RNAPII than the cleavage and polyadenylation pathway.
source: Even so, our data suggests that Integrator influences a greater volume of antisense RNAPII than the cleavage and polyadenylation pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing RBBP6 and INTS11 depletion effects.

claim: U1 promotes RNAPII elongation and shields transcription from early termination via the PAS-dependent mechanism and the Restrictor complex.
source: U1 promotes RNAPII elongation and shields transcription from early termination via the PAS-dependent mechanism and the Restrictor complex (Kaida et al., 2010; Estell et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The lack of U1 sites may limit RNAPII elongation and render it sensitive to Integrator (or Restrictor).
source: Nevertheless, the lack of U1 sites may limit RNAPII elongation and render it sensitive to Integrator (or Restrictor).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the role of U1 in protecting from attenuation.

claim: U1-mediated antagonism of INTS11 contributes to promoter directionality.
source: Indeed, while this paper was under consideration, U1-mediated antagonism of INTS11 was suggested to contribute to promoter directionality (Yang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recently published work.

claim: sPOINT demonstrates more efficient sense transcription initiation, which establishes directionality.
source: sPOINT demonstrates more efficient sense transcription initiation, which establishes directionality.
evidence: This is concluded from sPOINT-seq data in Figure 3.

claim: In the sense direction, CDK9 activity prevents attenuation by Integrator to favour productive elongation.
source: In the sense direction, CDK9 activity prevents attenuation by Integrator to favour productive elongation, whereas antisense transcription is hypersensitive to INTS11 and terminates early.
evidence: This is concluded from POINT-seq experiments showing differential INTS11 sensitivity.

claim: Antisense transcription is hypersensitive to INTS11 and terminates early.
source: In the sense direction, CDK9 activity prevents attenuation by Integrator to favour productive elongation, whereas antisense transcription is hypersensitive to INTS11 and terminates early.
evidence: This is concluded from POINT-seq experiments showing strong antisense effects of INTS11 loss.

claim: INTS11 occupies most promoters.
source: As INTS11 occupies most promoters and CDK9 activity is near-universally required to achieve protein-coding transcription, this model can generally explain how directionality is initiated and maintained.
evidence: This is based on published literature about Integrator localization.

claim: CDK9 activity is near-universally required to achieve protein-coding transcription.
source: As INTS11 occupies most promoters and CDK9 activity is near-universally required to achieve protein-coding transcription, this model can generally explain how directionality is initiated and maintained.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CDK9's role in transcription.

claim: The model of opposing INTS11 and CDK9 activities can generally explain how directionality is initiated and maintained.
source: As INTS11 occupies most promoters and CDK9 activity is near-universally required to achieve protein-coding transcription, this model can generally explain how directionality is initiated and maintained.
